title: Hangover Fatigue: Why You're Tired for Days and How to Recover
excerpt: Why a hangover leaves you exhausted, why the tiredness can last two or three days, what actually helps you recover, and when fatigue after drinking needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Why hangovers leave you exhausted, why the tiredness can last for days, what actually helps you recover, and when fatigue after drinking needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** hangover fatigue is mostly a sleep problem wearing a hangover costume. Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then breaks up the second half of the night, cuts into dream (REM) sleep, and leaves you running on a short, shallow night. Add the body's inflammatory response to alcohol, some dehydration, a disrupted body clock, and often a late meal or no meal, and you get the heavy, drained, can't-focus tiredness that can hang around well after the headache is gone. For most people it fades within a day. Feeling tired for two or three days after a big night is common, especially after a long weekend, a late finish, or as you get older. Fatigue that lasts longer than that, or that comes with the warning signs below, is worth a call to a doctor.

**The quick fixes that actually help:** drink water steadily through the day, eat a real meal with carbohydrates and protein, get outside into daylight, move gently (a 20 to 30 minute walk), keep caffeine moderate and early, take a short nap if you must, and go to bed at your normal time rather than very early or very late. No pill or drink erases the sleep debt. The fastest way out is one good night of sleep without alcohol.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangover tiredness is unpleasant but harmless. **Get medical help** if the fatigue lasts more than three days after you stopped drinking, keeps coming back even on weeks you don't drink, or comes with any of these: yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, chest pain, fainting, a very fast or irregular heartbeat, confusion, or severe weakness. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if someone is hard to wake, confused, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or unwell when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. Tell a doctor plainly; it is very treatable and they see it often. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Am I So Tired After Drinking?

Researchers who study hangovers (including the international Alcohol Hangover Research Group) list fatigue and sleepiness among the most commonly reported hangover symptoms, alongside headache, thirst, and trouble concentrating. In many surveys of drinkers, tiredness tops the list. That makes sense once you see how many separate things alcohol does to your body overnight. No single cause explains it. Several stack up.

### 1. Alcohol wrecks the second half of your night

Alcohol is a sedative, so it often helps you fall asleep faster. That's the part people notice. What they don't notice is what happens a few hours later. As your liver clears the alcohol, your brain swings the other way. Sleep becomes lighter and more broken, you wake up more often (even if you don't remember it), and you may surface very early and struggle to drop back off.

Alcohol also suppresses REM sleep, the dreaming stage that matters for mood, memory, and feeling mentally refreshed. Sleep scientists have documented this pattern for decades: more deep sleep early, less REM, and more disruption later in the night. The net result is that eight hours in bed after drinking can feel like five. You can read the details in our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025), and if you're lying awake at 4 a.m., see [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### 2. You probably slept less to begin with

Nights out tend to run late. If you got to bed at 2 a.m. and your alarm, your kids, or the sunlight woke you at 7, you're short on hours before alcohol has done anything to the quality of that sleep. Hangover fatigue is often ordinary sleep loss multiplied by poor sleep quality.

### 3. Your body is running an inflammatory response

Studies of hangovers have found raised levels of cytokines, which are the chemical messengers your immune system uses to coordinate inflammation. These are the same signals that make you feel tired, achy, and foggy when you have a cold or the flu. Researchers increasingly think this immune response is a central part of why a hangover makes you feel generally ill and wiped out, not just thirsty. It's one reason hangover fatigue can feel like you're "coming down with something."

### 4. Acetaldehyde and the work of clearing alcohol

Your liver breaks alcohol down first into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, then into acetate. Acetaldehyde is more harmful than alcohol itself and is linked to flushing, nausea, and feeling unwell. Clearing it, and repairing the minor stress it causes, is work your body does overnight and into the morning. The process also produces oxidative stress, a kind of chemical wear and tear on cells. None of this is dramatic for an occasional drinker, but it adds to the sense of being drained.

### 5. Dehydration, but probably less than you think

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Being even mildly dehydrated can make you feel tired, headachy, and dizzy. That said, research comparing hangover severity with measures of hydration has found only a weak link. Dehydration makes a hangover worse, but drinking lots of water doesn't fix the tiredness by itself. More on this in [does alcohol dehydrate you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 6. Blood sugar dips and skipped meals

Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases glucose, particularly if you drank on an empty stomach or skipped breakfast the next day. A dip in blood sugar can leave you shaky, weak, irritable, and tired. The evidence that low blood sugar drives most hangovers is mixed, but for anyone who drank without eating and then didn't eat in the morning, food often makes a noticeable difference. People with diabetes need to be especially careful here; see our [alcohol and blood sugar guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

### 7. Your brain's rebound

Alcohol boosts the calming GABA system and dampens the excitatory glutamate system. When it wears off, the brain is briefly out of balance in the other direction. That rebound is part of why people feel restless, anxious, and on edge the day after (the "hangxiety" many people describe), and being keyed up while also exhausted is a particularly draining combination. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers the anxious side of this.

### 8. Everything else that came with the night

Loud music, dancing, standing for hours, smoking or being around smoke, very salty or very rich food late at night, and a body clock pushed several hours out of place all contribute. Some drinks, especially darker spirits and red wine, contain more congeners (by-products of fermentation and aging), and some studies suggest these are linked to worse hangovers.

## Hangover Fatigue for Days: Why It Can Last Two or Three Days

Plenty of people expect a hangover to be a one-morning event and are surprised when they still feel flat on day two or three. This is common, and there are a few clear reasons.

**Sleep debt doesn't clear in one night.** If you lost several hours across Friday and Saturday, one decent Sunday night may only partly pay that back. And if the hangover itself caused a nap at 4 p.m., you may sleep badly that night too. Many "three-day hangovers" are really a chain of short or broken nights.

**Your body clock got shifted.** Staying up late, sleeping in, and spending the day indoors with the curtains closed all push your internal clock later. That's essentially a small dose of jet lag. Getting back on schedule can take a couple of days, during which you feel groggy in the morning and alert at the wrong times.

**Several nights in a row compound.** A wedding weekend, a holiday, a work conference, or a bachelor or bachelorette trip often means drinking on consecutive nights. Each night adds more sleep disruption and more recovery work, and the effect builds. Day three after a three-night stretch is a very different thing from the morning after one night out.

**Recovery may simply be slower with age.** Many people say their hangovers last longer than they used to. The research picture on age and hangovers is not settled, but older adults often sleep more lightly to begin with, and alcohol's effects on sleep can hit harder. Our guide on [why hangovers get worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age) goes through the likely reasons.

**Mood dips can linger.** Alcohol's rebound effects on brain chemistry, plus poor sleep, can leave you low, unmotivated, and tired for a day or two. People often describe this as the "Sunday scaries" or the "Tuesday blues" after a big weekend.

If this sounds like you, our article on the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) covers the longer version in detail, and [how long does a hangover last](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) gives a broader timeline.

## How Long Does Hangover Fatigue Last?

For most people, hangover symptoms peak in the morning when blood alcohol returns to zero and ease over the course of the day. A rough guide:

- **After a moderate night with decent sleep:** the tiredness usually lifts by the afternoon or evening.
- **After a heavy night or a very late finish:** expect to feel low on energy for the whole day and possibly part of the next.
- **After several nights in a row:** two to three days of below-par energy is common, mostly from accumulated sleep debt and a shifted body clock.

A practical rule: if you feel noticeably better each day, that's normal recovery. If you're three or more days past your last drink and not improving, or you feel worse, something else may be going on and it's worth checking with a doctor.

## Is It Hangover Fatigue or Something Else?

It's easy to blame every tired Monday on the weekend. Sometimes that's right. Sometimes the drinking is only part of the story. It's worth thinking about other causes if:

- **You're tired most days, not just after drinking.** Common causes of ongoing fatigue include iron deficiency or anemia, thyroid problems, vitamin B12 or vitamin D deficiency, depression, diabetes, and simply not getting enough sleep week in, week out.
- **You snore loudly, gasp during sleep, or wake with a dry mouth and headache.** These can be signs of sleep apnea, a condition where breathing repeatedly stops during sleep. Alcohol relaxes the throat muscles and can make apnea worse. If that sounds familiar, mention it to a doctor; a sleep study can check.
- **The tiredness started after a new medication.** Many medicines (some antidepressants, antihistamines, sleep aids, pain medicines, and others) cause drowsiness on their own, and alcohol can make that much stronger. If you take medication and feel unusually tired after drinking, ask your pharmacist or doctor about the combination.
- **You have a fever, a sore throat, or body aches beyond a typical hangover.** You may actually be coming down with an infection. Our page on [hangover fever](/never-hungover/hangover-fever) explains how to tell the difference.
- **You feel foggy and slow for days.** Some brain fog after drinking is normal, but if it doesn't lift, see [brain fog after drinking](/never-hungover/brain-fog-after-drinking) and talk to a doctor if it persists.

If you regularly drink a lot and feel drained most of the time, alcohol may be affecting your sleep, liver, and mood more than you realize. That's a good reason to have an honest chat with a doctor, who can check basic blood tests and give you a straightforward picture.

## How to Get Rid of Hangover Fatigue

There's no shortcut that cancels lost sleep, but you can make the day a lot more bearable and set yourself up to recover faster. These are the steps with the best mix of common sense and evidence behind them.

### Rehydrate steadily, not all at once

Drink water through the morning rather than forcing down a liter in one go. If you were sick, sweated a lot, or feel dizzy when you stand, an oral rehydration drink or an electrolyte drink can help replace salts as well as water. Clear, pale-yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're back on track. Our comparison of [electrolyte drinks for hangovers](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) looks at the common options.

### Eat a proper meal

Food is one of the most underrated fixes for hangover tiredness, especially if you drank on an empty stomach. Aim for something that combines carbohydrates (toast, oats, rice, potatoes, fruit) with protein (eggs, yogurt, chicken, beans). This gives you steady energy rather than a sugar spike and crash. If your stomach is unsettled, start small with plain toast, crackers, bananas, or broth and build up. See our [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) for ideas.

### Get daylight early

Natural light is the strongest signal your body clock has. Going outside in the morning, even on a cloudy day, helps reset your internal clock, makes you feel more alert during the day, and makes it easier to fall asleep at a normal time that night. Ten to thirty minutes outside is a good target. Sitting in a dark room all day feels comforting but tends to drag the grogginess out.

### Move gently

Hard exercise on a hangover is usually a bad idea, since you may be dehydrated and your heart rate can already be elevated. Light movement, like a walk, an easy bike ride, or some stretching, can lift your energy and mood without adding strain. Stop if you feel dizzy, sick, or your heart is racing. More in [does exercise help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover).

### Use caffeine carefully

A normal cup of coffee or tea can help you feel more awake and may ease a caffeine-withdrawal headache if you usually drink coffee. Two cautions. First, caffeine masks tiredness, it doesn't fix it, so you're still impaired even if you feel more alert. Second, caffeine late in the day will make tonight's sleep worse, which drags the fatigue into tomorrow. A sensible approach is to keep to your usual amount and have it before early afternoon. Our [coffee for hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) guide covers the pros and cons, and if you're tempted by something stronger, read [energy drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/energy-drink-for-hangover) first.

### Nap smart, or not at all

A short nap of about 20 to 30 minutes in the early afternoon can take the edge off without ruining your night. Long naps late in the day are the classic trap: you wake up groggy, then can't sleep at bedtime, and the cycle continues. If you're very sleep-deprived, a single longer nap early in the afternoon is better than a late one. Our article on [whether sleep helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-sleep-help-a-hangover) looks at this in more depth.

### Go to bed at your normal time

The best single thing you can do for hangover fatigue is get one solid, alcohol-free night of sleep. Aim to go to bed at your usual time, in a dark, cool room, without screens right before bed. Going to bed very early can backfire if you wake at 3 a.m. Going to bed late pushes your clock further out. A normal bedtime and a normal wake-up time the next morning is the fastest route back to feeling like yourself.

### Skip the "hair of the dog"

Having another drink to feel better only postpones the problem. It adds more alcohol for your body to clear, disrupts another night of sleep, and tends to make the eventual crash worse. There is no good evidence that drinking more relieves a hangover. Regularly needing a drink to feel normal the morning after is also a sign worth taking seriously and mentioning to a doctor.

### What about painkillers and other medicines?

If you have a headache or body aches along with the tiredness, a standard dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever can make the day more comfortable, but none of them treat fatigue. Each has trade-offs after drinking: ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) needs care because of how it's processed by the liver. Read our guides on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [the best medicine for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-medicine-for-hangover) before reaching for one. Avoid sleeping pills or sedating antihistamines on the night you drink; combining them with alcohol increases drowsiness and slows breathing.

## Don't Drive or Do Risky Work While You're Wiped Out

This part matters more than most people realize. Studies of next-day performance have found that people with a hangover can show impaired attention, slower reactions, and worse driving, even after their blood alcohol is back to zero. Driving simulator research has found hangover-related impairment comparable in some measures to driving with alcohol still in the blood.

Fatigue is a big part of that. Feeling "fine" after a coffee doesn't mean your reaction time has recovered. If you're very tired the day after drinking, avoid driving if you can, be careful with machinery, ladders, or anything where a lapse in attention could hurt someone, and give yourself extra time and margin for error at work. If you had a lot to drink late at night, you may also still have alcohol in your system in the morning.

## How to Avoid Hangover Fatigue Next Time

Since most hangover fatigue comes from disrupted sleep, the best prevention protects your sleep and limits how much alcohol your body has to deal with overnight.

- **Drink less, and pace it.** This is the one with by far the most evidence. Fewer drinks, spread out over the evening, means less sleep disruption and a lighter next day. Alternating each alcoholic drink with a glass of water or a non-alcoholic drink is an easy way to do this.
- **Stop drinking a few hours before bed.** The closer your last drink is to bedtime, the more alcohol is still in your system as you sleep. Finishing earlier gives your body a head start and tends to mean less disruption in the second half of the night.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed and helps steady your blood sugar.
- **Protect your sleep window.** If you know it's a late night, plan to sleep in a little the next morning, or at least avoid an early alarm. Keep your bedroom dark and cool.
- **Choose lighter drinks.** Clear spirits and lighter drinks tend to contain fewer congeners than dark spirits, red wine, and some whiskies. This doesn't change the effect of the alcohol itself, but some people notice a difference. Our ranking of [least hangover-inducing alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) has the details.
- **Space out big nights.** Back-to-back nights of drinking are what turn a one-day hangover into a three-day slump. If you have a run of events, consider having alcohol-free nights in between.

For a fuller playbook, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits In (An Honest Take)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis) that's popular as a hangover supplement. Lab and animal research suggests it may support the breakdown of alcohol and acetaldehyde and may act on the brain's GABA receptors, and one well-known rat study found it reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal. Human evidence is much more limited. There is no good evidence that DHM fixes lost sleep or removes hangover fatigue, and it doesn't make it safe to drive or to drink more.

If you want to try it as part of a sensible approach (eating, pacing, water, and an earlier last drink), common picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. If you take prescription medication, check with your pharmacist or doctor before adding any supplement.
Tiredness is one symptom of many. Our full guide to [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) covers the rest and explains which ones are worth paying attention to.

## The Bottom Line

- Hangover fatigue mostly comes from short, broken, low-REM sleep, plus inflammation, mild dehydration, blood sugar dips, and a shifted body clock.
- Most people feel better within a day. Two or three days of low energy is common after a heavy night or several nights in a row.
- Water, a proper meal, morning daylight, a gentle walk, moderate early caffeine, a short nap at most, and a normal bedtime are the most useful steps.
- Don't drive or do risky tasks while you're wiped out, even if your blood alcohol is back to zero.
- Fatigue lasting more than three days, fatigue that happens even when you don't drink, or tiredness with yellow skin, chest pain, confusion, or repeated vomiting needs a doctor. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety when you stop after daily heavy drinking can be withdrawal, and you should get medical care for it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why am I so tired after drinking alcohol?**

Mainly because alcohol disrupts your sleep. It helps you fall asleep, but as your body clears it, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, and dream (REM) sleep is reduced. On top of that, your immune system releases inflammatory signals that make you feel run down, you may be mildly dehydrated, your blood sugar can dip if you didn't eat, and late nights shift your body clock. Together these leave you feeling drained even after a full night in bed.

**How long does hangover fatigue last?**

For most people it eases by the afternoon or evening of the day after drinking. After a heavy night or a very late finish it can last the whole day and part of the next. After several nights of drinking in a row, two to three days of low energy is common, mainly from built-up sleep debt. If you're three or more days past your last drink and not improving, check with a doctor.

**Why am I still tired two or three days after drinking?**

Usually it's accumulated sleep debt and a shifted body clock. A late night, a disrupted sleep, a long afternoon nap, and then another poor night can chain together. Drinking on several nights in a row, getting older, and the low mood that can follow a big weekend all make it last longer. Steady daylight, normal meals, and a regular bedtime help you reset faster.

**How do I get rid of hangover fatigue fast?**

There is no instant fix, but the most useful steps are drinking water steadily, eating a meal with carbohydrates and protein, getting outside in daylight, taking a gentle walk, having your usual coffee early in the day, limiting naps to about 20 to 30 minutes, and going to bed at your normal time. One full night of alcohol-free sleep does more than anything else.

**Should I nap if I have a hangover?**

A short nap of about 20 to 30 minutes in the early afternoon can help. Long or late naps often backfire, because they make it harder to sleep that night, which drags the tiredness into the next day. If you're very short on sleep, take any longer nap early in the afternoon rather than in the evening.

**Is it safe to drive when I have hangover fatigue?**

It's best to avoid it. Research on next-day performance has found that people with a hangover can have slower reactions, worse attention, and impaired driving even when their blood alcohol is back to zero. Coffee can make you feel more alert without restoring your reaction time. After a late, heavy night you may also still have alcohol in your system in the morning.

**When should I worry about feeling tired after drinking?**

See a doctor if the fatigue lasts more than three days, happens even on weeks you don't drink, or comes with yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, chest pain, fainting, repeated vomiting, or confusion. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or having a seizure, call 911. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be withdrawal and needs medical care.

**Does DHM help with hangover fatigue?**

There is no good evidence that DHM restores lost sleep or removes hangover tiredness. Lab and animal studies suggest it may support alcohol metabolism, but human data are limited. If you try it, treat it as one small part of a sensible approach that includes eating, pacing your drinks, drinking water, and finishing your last drink well before bed.
